Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

vignette:
Liam, a 29-year-old Coast Guard officer, sat across from the clinician, his posture rigid despite the comfortable armchair. He had finally decided to seek help, almost eight months after an incident that had fundamentally altered his sense of safety and self.

The mugging had occurred late one evening as Liam walked home from a friend's place in a quiet residential area. He remembered the suddenness of it: a shadow detaching from an alleyway, a rough hand clamping over his mouth, the metallic glint of a knife pressed against his ribs. He had been disoriented, shoved against a brick wall, his wallet and phone ripped from his pockets. The assailant’s breath had been hot and stale against his ear, a low growl of threats. It had been over in moments, leaving him alone, shaken, and utterly violated on the cold pavement. The streetlights had seemed to mock his vulnerability, casting long, accusing shadows.

Since that night, Liam often found his mind grappling with what had happened, but the images and sensations came to him in disconnected pieces. He would see a flash of the knife, feel the sudden shove, hear a muffled demand, but these fragments refused to coalesce into a coherent narrative. It was as if the incident had exploded into a thousand shards, and he could only ever grasp a few at a time, never the whole.

When he tried to talk about the incident, the words seemed to fail him completely. It was as if the frightening event resided in a part of him that language couldn't reach, leaving him struggling to articulate the profound impact it had. He would start a sentence, only for it to trail off, the experience too vast and formless for verbal expression. This struggle was particularly evident when his girlfriend, Sarah, gently encouraged him to share more, and Liam would find himself unable to bridge the gap between his internal experience and words.

Sometimes, a detail would surface, clear and distinct, but it was accompanied by a chilling emotional numbness. He could recall the specific pattern on the assailant's worn jacket, or the cold, damp feel of the brick wall against his back, yet it felt as though he was an detached observer, watching a scene unfold that had happened to someone else entirely. These moments of recall were unsettling in their very lack of emotion, leaving him feeling disconnected from his own past, as if a vital piece of his personal history belonged to a stranger.

His daily life as a Coast Guard officer, demanding focus and precision, continued around him. The structured environment of his work, with its clear protocols and chain of command, offered a stark contrast to the internal chaos he experienced. He maintained his duties, navigating the practicalities of his role, but internally, the struggle with his memories persisted, a quiet undercurrent to his disciplined exterior.

Liam knew he could no longer ignore the way his memories functioned. The fragmented and emotionally distant nature of his recollections, alongside his inability to articulate what had happened, were a persistent and unsettling aspect of his daily life. He simply wanted to understand what had transpired, and why his own memory felt so alien. He hoped that by speaking with someone, he might finally find a way to make sense of the pieces, or at least to navigate the numb detachment that often accompanied his recollections of the night that had changed everything.
